item.title: Interstitial ad frequency: tutorials don't count – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

We set interstitial frequency from device timelines, and tutorials don't count

Once the three tutorial puzzles stopped counting toward ads, the first interstitial in puzzle mode moved to after the third real puzzle. We chose what to count by reading ad logs from fresh installs in time order.

A fresh install that had not played a single real puzzle got a full-screen interstitial 91 seconds after launch. It happened on October 4, 2026, on a Galaxy S21, when a scripted, human-paced run on a test-ad release build finished the three tutorial puzzles in Block Turn and tapped Next. The operator decided the same day that tutorials would no longer count toward ads, and according to the commit message the first interstitial on the emulator moved from 181 s to 314 s. The same runs showed classic mode at 1.4 full-screen ads per 10 minutes against 3.3 for the puzzle mode, so a classic game over now counts as two runs toward the interstitial.

Sources: the game repository's ad plan and launch rehearsal documents, PRD v2.1 §11.2, git commits 2a4b820, df52a51, 575aaa1, 73a12ad, e430133 and 85e3685, the session script block_session_sim.py and the simulator block_revenue_sim.py. Checked on November 1, 2026.

On a fresh install, the first interstitial came before any real puzzle

Block Turn shows an interstitial only when a player taps Next, Play again or Home after a finished run. The numbers lived in one place (Money.RULES): at least 3 finished runs, 2 runs since the last interstitial, 90 s since the session started, 120 s since the previous full-screen ad, at most 5 per session and 20 per day, and only if an ad was already loaded. Here "full-screen ad" means interstitials, rewarded ads and app open ads together. The PRD (v2.1 §11.2) rules out an interstitial within the first three finished runs and the first 90 seconds of a session, and hides the banner on the tutorial puzzles and the first three runs.

Every run on October 4 started from cleared app data. The session script (block_session_sim.py) plays scripted runs, or personas, each with a fixed mode and pace range, and reads ad impressions from the SDK log. On the S21, the first interstitial came at 91 s, on Next after tutorial R003. The emulator finished the tutorials in 64 s; its first interstitial came after R004, at 181 s. Two other emulator personas (mixed and return) got their first one at 158 s and 134 s.

The three tutorials had already met the 3-run gate

The function that counted finished runs did not tell tutorials apart. In the first version of the app, written with the coding agent (cd62087), Money.onRunEnded() added every tutorial solve to the banner's run count and to the interstitial's win count, exactly like a real run. By the time the third tutorial ended, "3 finished runs" was already true.

Both the 3-run gate and the 90-second grace were meant to protect a new player. The three tutorials take 64 to 90 seconds, so the two guards opened at nearly the same time instead of adding up. The first ad's timing then depended on how fast the tutorials were cleared. The emulator met the 3-run gate at 64 s but was still inside the 90-second grace, so its ad waited for the next run, R004; on the S21 the grace was nearly over when R003 ended, so the ad came right after the tutorials.

The numbers came from documents. The monetization design for our other game in the same repository, Arrow Knots, cited industry advice to hold the first interstitial back from the session start and picked a 90-second grace; Block Turn's PRD wrote the same 90 s and passed it to the shared pacing module (Pacer). The session script first arrived in the launch prep commit 575aaa1 on October 4. Before it, the repository has no record of anyone looking at the first few minutes on a time axis.

A test written with the agent had locked the behavior in. The device E2E suite committed that morning (4fa0dfa) checked "banner shown from R004" as a pass condition in scenario S1. Under the PRD, R004 is the first real puzzle and should have no banner. The first draft of the launch plan raised the tutorial problem from a simulation only, and the cross-check disputed it. Once the device logs came in, the ad plan marked the issue as confirmed by measurement.

Run length decided which rule set the pace

In a 12-minute run of the three-move puzzle persona on the emulator, interstitials appeared at 181, 322, 465 and 611 s: gaps of 141 to 146 s, or 3.3 per 10 minutes. A puzzle takes about a minute, so "every 2 runs" was always met first, and the 120-second gap was what held the pace.

Classic went the other way. In a 14-minute S21 session, tutorials included, classic produced 2 runs (150 moves); the ad plan puts a run at about five minutes. The only interstitial was the one right after the tutorials. Counting the one rewarded revive the script accepted, the session still had just 1.4 full-screen ads per 10 minutes. Two classic runs take about ten minutes, so in classic the every-2-runs gate, not the 120 s gap, set the pace.

The launch plan's simulator (block_revenue_sim.py) assumed a 90-second classic run, while the comment on that same line quoted the classic supply experiment's human target of 4 to 10 minutes. It also kept each interstitial on screen for 15 s; the session script closed them after 5 to 8 s, like a person. Replaying the puzzle persona in the simulator gave 4.09 interstitials in 12 minutes, matching the 4 measured, but a median gap of 162 s against the measured 141 to 146 s. Running the same persona command again on November 1 gave 4.09 and 162 s.

Tutorials excluded, classic counted twice, a 6-run gate dropped

Commit e430133, on the evening of October 4, carries the operator's three frequency decisions (the fourth item in that list is the banner slot rule below). Its message files them as "user decisions, from device measurements". The store listing's ad notice was changed in the same commit to say there is no banner and no between-run ad on the tutorials and the first three runs.

  • Tutorials no longer count toward the banner or the interstitial. In puzzle mode a new player sees neither before three real runs.
  • A classic game over counts as two runs toward the interstitial: the code adds two wins. So in classic the interstitial can come from the second game over for a new player, then after every game over, while the banner still waits for three runs. The 120 s gap and the session and daily caps stay, and the ad plan estimated that classic players would go from 1.4 to about 2 per 10 minutes.
  • No app open ad when the player returns in the middle of a run (a classic move made, or a puzzle piece placed and the puzzle not yet over).
fun onRunEnded(tutorial: Boolean = false, classic: Boolean = false) {
    if (tutorial) return
    runsEnded++
    prefs.edit().putInt(K_RUNS, runsEnded).apply()
    if (!enabled) return
    ads.onWin()
    if (classic) ads.onWin()
}

Raising the first-interstitial threshold from 3 runs to 6 would have been a one-constant change. The ad plan advised against it: once players who skip tutorials or abandon runs are in the mix, a raw count gives a grace of uneven length, so it recommended excluding tutorial solves instead. An interstitial after every run was ruled out because the 120 s gap already set the pace; only classic, with its long runs, moved to every game over. Removing the interstitial on the classic result screen's Home button was considered; the ad plan recommended keeping it, treating the break after a score screen as an allowed placement, and the code was left as is. The genre habit of an ad after every game over, as in Block Blast, was one input to the classic change.

When you set numbers meant to protect new players, leave tutorial levels out of the ad counters. Then check on a freshly installed device, from the log, at which second and after which run the first ad actually appears.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The banner slot rule changed five times, between an empty strip and a shifting layout

From October 3 to 5, each change fixed what the previous rule left behind, and the first one (2a4b820) was made in the shared module before Block Turn existed.

Time (KST)CommitBanner slot ruleWhat it left
Oct 3 16:382a4b820No space until ads may be requested (consent pending or refused)Empty strip on an offline device with consent already stored
Oct 4 02:05df52a51Zero height until the first ad actually arrivesA late fill pushed the board down (S21 classic, y 416 to 620)
Oct 4 17:14575aaa1Slot reserved up frontOffline empty strip (listed as a drawback in the ad plan)
Oct 4 19:07e430133Reserved only after a banner has filled in this processThe first fill in each process pushed the HUD down and put the banner where the home chip was
Oct 5 12:5285e3685Reserved from the first frame on every screen; collapses only on a failed loadOffline, an empty strip shows briefly, then folds

The last change (85e3685) lets the layout move only away from the ad: when the banner collapses, content moves up, and the ad never slides down onto the home and undo chips a finger is reaching for. The same commit stops reserving the slot and requesting ads after a failed load for 1, 2, 4 and up to 10 minutes, so the empty strip shows up less often.

Block Turn launched without Firebase, so D1 and D7 went unmeasured at launch

A device timeline shows when ads appear and how often, not whether players stay. Analytics arrived only on October 11, in the vc4 commit ae9cd16, and there is still no remote config as of November 1. GA4 has tracked D1 since, but no one has compared it across the rule change yet. The ad plan gives PRD compliance and first impressions as the reasons for excluding tutorials, noting there is no number for how much retention would improve.

An app with remote config, analytics and enough players has a better basis: a 50/50 A/B test that changes frequency alone. Our PRD (§11.3) planned a 5% holdback of new players with no interstitials, but the ad plan dropped it because telling a 12% D7 from a 10% D7 at a 1:19 split would take about 42,000 installs; it plans a 50/50 single-variable A/B once there is scale. Without remote config, every frequency change in Block Turn needs an app update and a store review.

Each persona ran once, at a pace drawn from fixed ranges. That is not the spread of real player speeds, and the same rules already gave first ads at 91 s and 181 s. The builds used test ads, so fill rates may differ from live ads. The code shows an interstitial only when one is preloaded, so live counts can match these numbers or fall below them. What real players did in the first chapter is in Puzzle game day-one churn: the walls in chapter 1.

After pm clear, 12 to 15 minutes of logs, with S11 before S10

  1. Build with test ad IDs only. For a release build, keep minification on and keep only the ad and run-end log lines. Count the test and real IDs in the dex as in Why R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in a release AAB. Never drive a real-ID build with automated taps; those are invalid clicks.
  2. Have the app log one line each time it shows a full-screen ad (something like ads: show interstitial) and one line each time a run ends.
  3. Clear the app data for a fresh-install state, clear the log, and note the start time from the device clock.
  4. Play 12 to 15 minutes at human speed. Our session script spent 20 to 60 s thinking per puzzle, took 1.5 to 3.5 s per classic move, watched each interstitial for 5 to 8 s and accepted half of the revive offers. Run each mode separately.
  5. Read off the first full-screen ad, the gaps between interstitials, and the full-screen ads per 10 minutes (count / minutes x 10).
  6. Check the mid-run return rule by order. Make one move, go home, wait 250 s (longer than the 4-minute threshold) and come back: no app open ad (S11). Then make the same return from the home screen: one should appear (S10). Run S11 first: the day's app open cap (2 a day) is still unused then, which leaves the mid-run rule as the only reason no ad appeared.
  7. After changing a rule, rerun the same persona and compare.
adb shell pm clear <package>
adb logcat -c
adb shell date +%s.%N        # start time, device clock
adb logcat -v epoch -s ads:D GAME:D > session.log
# python timeline.py session.log <start time> <minutes played>
import re, sys
log, t0, minutes = sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2]), float(sys.argv[3])
rx = re.compile(r"\s*([\d.]+)\s+\d+\s+\d+\s+\w\s+ads\s*:\s+show (\w+)")
shows = [(round(float(m[1]) - t0), m[2]) for m in map(rx.match, open(log, errors="ignore")) if m]
inter = [t for t, kind in shows if kind.lower() == "interstitial"]
print("first", shows[:1], "gaps", [b - a for a, b in zip(inter, inter[1:])],
      "per10min", round(len(shows) / (minutes / 10), 2))

The S21 and classic numbers after the change are still missing

As of November 1, the repository has no device re-measurement of the S21's first interstitial after tutorials stopped counting, and none of the classic rate after a game over started counting twice. The 314 s figure exists only in the commit message; its raw log was not kept in the repository, and neither the persona nor the build it used is recorded. The commit comment says there is no between-run ad in the first three runs, but in the code a classic-only player becomes eligible after the second game over. On November 1 the operator kept the code and decided to drop that sentence from the store notice. Checking the first interstitial by hand on a real-ID build is still listed for the operator in the launch rehearsal document.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

When should a puzzle game show its first interstitial?

In Block Turn's puzzle mode, with tutorials excluded, the first interstitial can come after three real runs once 90 s of the session have passed; in classic, where a game over counts twice, after the second game over. On the emulator on October 4, 2026, it came at 314 s, per the commit message.

Does the ad gap or "every N levels" decide how often interstitials show?

Run length decides. If two runs take longer than the 120 s gap, the every-2-runs gate sets the pace; otherwise the gap does. In the puzzle mode, where a run takes about a minute, the 120 s gap set the pace; in classic, where a run takes about five minutes, the every-2-runs gate did, so Block Turn now counts a classic game over twice.

How do I avoid an empty banner space when the device is offline?

Collapse the slot in the failed-load callback, then hold off on both the slot and the request for a while. Block Turn waits 1 minute, doubling up to 10 minutes. We dropped the zero-height-until-filled approach because a late fill pushed the board down.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Subagent prompt rules and five cut-off agents – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

Six hard rules in one subagent brief, and five agents cut off by usage limits

In the four cases we can check, the report each cut-off subagent had been told to create first was still empty. The next agent picked up the work from the logs, screenshots and edited files left on disk.

Five subagents working on the store release of our Flutter P2P chat app stopped before finishing. It happened between September 7 and 10, 2026: three hit the session limit, one hit the weekly usage limit, and one stopped for a reason nobody wrote down. Rule 6 of the shared brief said to create the report early and update it as the work went on. In all four cases where a committed copy of the report exists, every body section was still empty apart from the after-fix test's environment section. The agents that took over read git diffs, logcat files and screenshots instead, and the one task with no files on record, a full inventory of UI strings, was measured again from scratch.

Sources: the app repository's git history (e450c09, d464dc4, 7f52466, 9f03e7a, dca6cf9, af912bf, e9d882f, 67edc8d, 8dacf19), the shared brief and the three briefs that followed it, 17 analysis reports and 42 fix reports. Times are commit times in KST, except the start and end of handover work, which come from the reports. Report line counts and finding counts were recounted from git on November 1, 2026.

Five agents stopped between September 7 and 10

The analysis round landed at 23:10 on September 7 as commit e450c09: one shared brief of 33 lines and 17 analysis reports. Report 14, the emulator lab, was a 19-line skeleton. Its header said it was in progress with partial results, and every section read "(in progress)". Forty-seven minutes later, in d464dc4, the same file had 71 lines and a new header: the first agent had left device scripts and two install screenshots and stopped, and a second agent had carried on from there.

At 09:08 on September 8, commit dca6cf9 went in with the message "agent interrupted by session limit; to be continued". The agent consolidating the docs had stopped at the session limit with a 19-line skeleton report. The four docs it had already edited (the project's CLAUDE.md, the release plan, the security notes and the threat model) went into that commit as partial work. The same commit carried the result folders of the lab agent that, by its report, had started the after-fix end-to-end test at 00:24 that day. It had also hit the session limit, and its report had the environment table filled in and sections 2 to 8 marked "(in progress)".

On September 9 the device recheck (H1) stopped at the weekly limit, and the orchestrator finished it by reading the raw evidence itself. On September 10 the string inventory (X1) was committed at 01:45 as an 8-line skeleton and came back at 04:34 with 1,046 lines. Its new header said the previous agent had stopped at the session limit without leaving any measurements, so everything had been measured again.

The 33-line brief lists no per-agent tasks

The brief has four parts: a one-line goal, verified facts about the environment, six hard rules, and a report format. Each agent's topic came separately; those prompts are not in the repository. The environment part names the Flutter version and which binary to run, the two Android emulators, and "no physical device, no Xcode or macOS". The six rules, paraphrased:

  1. Install no system packages and add no new packages. If one is needed, write "approval needed" in the report.
  2. Upload nothing anywhere. Outputs stay as files in the repository.
  3. During analysis, do not edit code under lib/, android/ or ios/. Write scripts and documents only.
  4. No blanket sed replacements. Move files to a scratch folder instead of rm -rf.
  5. When checking an outside policy, give the URL and the date you checked it. Mark guesses as guesses.
  6. Write the report in Korean, at the assigned path, create it early and update it as you go, "so that partial results survive if the session is cut off".

The report format has five sections: summary, what was checked, findings, fixes that can be applied now, and remaining unknowns. The findings table has six columns: ID, severity (Blocker, High, Medium or Low), description, evidence (file:line or URL), proposed fix, and how to verify it. IDs carry a prefix per topic, such as AND-, IOS-, SEC- or LAB-.

The prohibitions were used. At e450c09, 13 analysis reports contain "approval needed". The store readiness analysis listed an icon generator package as "approval needed (rule 1)", and the iOS project analysis noted that using it would mean adding a dev dependency that needs approval. The fix stage skipped the package and generated the icons with a script on the Python imaging library that was already installed. The release workflows were written but not run. The brief left running them to the main session, and the first successful iOS compile run is recorded in commit 9f03e7a at 00:27 the next day. Eight UI findings were left as 11 deliberately failing tests rather than code changes. Keeping the prohibitions in one file the agent reads every time is the same idea as A permission table for a scheduled AI agent.

The format held too. All 17 reports have the six-column table and the unknowns section, and the 16 that had a body listed 233 findings, 15 of them Blockers. The fix reports took their work by those IDs; the iOS platform fix report alone cites 38 of them. The severity scale did not hold. The iOS project analysis used Info, which the brief never defined, four times, and the dependency and lab analyses invented "Low (confirmed false positive)" and "Low~Medium".

Rule 6 left empty report bodies

The brief assumed that a report created early would hold partial results if the agent was cut off. In the four cases where a committed copy exists (the lab analysis, the after-fix test, the docs consolidation and the string inventory), every body section read "(in progress)", except the environment section of the after-fix test.

The after-fix test report came closest to the rule. Its header told readers that blank cells meant "not measured" if the session ended. When the session did end, every result table was blank. The raw and screens folders in the same commit held two logcat files (103,813 and 89,023 lines), the signalling server log, 43 screenshots and the raw timings of 11 messages. The template script, anchored on the wrong log line, paired only one of them and reported n=1, 11 ms.

Rule 6 asked agents to create the report and to update it, but never said how often, and the findings were never written to a file. As far as the record shows, they lived only in the agent's conversation context. None of the agents cut off in this round got to tidy up its report before it stopped. What was left on disk were the files that running commands and editing docs had produced along the way.

The next agent read git diff and the raw folder

Four of the five handovers continued on files the earlier session had left; the second lab analysis agent, too, started from the first one's device scripts and two install screenshots. The docs agent stopped with its edits uncommitted, because the fix-stage brief let only the main session commit. The main session committed that state as dca6cf9. The finished report, in af912bf at 00:06 on September 9, shows the next agent starting with git diff 7f52466..dca6cf9 to see what had been done. CLAUDE.md had every requested change, the security notes had 7 of 8, and nine other docs plus the store drafts were untouched. The new agent left the finished parts alone and completed 19 files.

The after-fix test was picked up by another lab agent at 23:15 on September 8, by its report, and finished 50 minutes later. It kept the raw files for build, install, connection and messaging, and ran only the remaining tests (lifecycle, blocking, data reset and so on). It did not measure the round trip again; it recalculated it from the burst of 10 messages the earlier session had already sent, using the correct log anchor (p50 61 ms, p95 74 ms). The report grew from 41 lines to 338. The device recheck had stopped after its evidence was essentially collected, so 85 screenshots and 8 kinds of logs on disk were enough for the orchestrator to write the verdict.

The string inventory was reading and judging, and the record shows no files left behind. Starting from the 8-line skeleton, the next agent parsed all 2,864 string literals in 93 files under lib/ again and judged the 464 that can appear on screen. The brief for that round still carried the update-as-you-go rule. The contrast checker recount from the same commit, 8dacf19, is in Our contrast checker skipped 40% of the text.

Put the path and timing for raw evidence in a subagent brief before you ask for a report.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The verify column corrected a backup prediction

The platform security analysis read the code and predicted that an app restored from Android auto backup would lose its Keystore key and become permanently unusable (SEC-2). The lab agent did what the row's verify column said: backed up, uninstalled, reinstalled and restored with bmgr. The app did not get stuck. After a key unwrap error it went back to the setup screen and created a new profile, and the old keys and chat history disappeared without a word (LAB-7). The proposed fix, turning backup off (allowBackup=false), was still needed after the test.

The fix-stage brief said to verify each proposed diff before applying it. The UI fix agent reported that three of diffs A to H were wrong or incomplete and applied corrected versions: what Theme.of returns inside a bottom sheet, how button labels shrink, and the fact that useSafeArea: true does not handle the bottom inset. The instructions were wrong once too. The port assignment in the after-fix test instructions did not match the direction of the adb forward chain, so each app would have dialled itself; the agent swapped them and noted the swap in its environment table.

Letting subagents commit, or always starting over

One way to protect against interruptions is to let each subagent commit its own work. This round ruled that out. Several agents were editing files in the same working tree at once, and a single git stash, or a git checkout that restores files, could wipe someone else's changes. The cost was that interrupted work sat uncommitted until the main session committed it. How sessions collided in one working tree is covered in Claude Code sessions in one repo: file owner table.

The taking-over agent can also always start from scratch. With files left, the device recheck only needed a new verdict from 85 screenshots and 8 kinds of logs, and the after-fix test was finished in 50 minutes by its report. With nothing left, the string inventory re-parsed all 2,864 literals. Writing the report once at the end is what rule 6 was meant to prevent, and for X1 the outcome was the same as if it had.

We found no sign in the record that separate briefs per agent were considered. In practice the three later briefs (fixes, fixes for review findings, and the full inventory) each point back to the shared brief ("applies unchanged", "follow") and add what changed at that stage. Besides rules such as "edit only the files you own", "do not commit" and "write tests that fail when the guard is removed", the review-fix brief added an identity-binding API contract and the inventory brief added a table of expected outputs.

Read-only tasks and severity values outside the scale

Handing over from files on disk only worked where the work produced files anyway. A task that only reads code and judges it, like the string inventory or a code review, leaves nothing behind.

This round's brief listed the four allowed severity values and defined each, and Info and Low~Medium still appeared. If a tool will count or sort by severity, do not stop at listing the values; check the reports when they arrive.

The environment section is machine-specific. This round had no physical device and no Mac, so running on iOS and on real hardware all went to the unknowns. You can reuse the brief's structure, but check that section again on your own machine. We cannot say how many defects these rules prevented, because there is no comparable round without them.

A brief template and the commands for a handover

This template merges the rules of the shared brief and the fix-stage brief, and adds a path for raw output and a unit of update.

# <round> shared brief (<date>)
Goal: <one line>
## Environment (verified only)
- Tool paths and versions: <...>
- Devices available: <...> / not available: <...>
## Do not
1. Install or add packages. If one is needed, write "approval needed"
2. Upload anything. Outputs are files in the repository only
3. Edit files you do not own. Put requests in "requests to other owners"
4. commit, stash or checkout (the main session commits)
5. Guess without saying so. Outside docs get a URL and a check date
## Output paths
- Report: <dir>/<NN>_<topic>.md
  Create it first; the first line is exactly "Status: in progress"
- Raw: <dir>/raw/<NN>_*
  Save command output, logs and screenshots as soon as you get them
- Add a table row each time one finding or one measurement is done
## Report format
Summary / What was checked / Findings / Remaining unknowns
| ID | Severity | Description | Evidence (file:line / URL) | Proposed fix | How to verify |
Severity is exactly one of Blocker, High, Medium, Low

When taking over, read git and the raw folder before the report.

  1. Find unfinished reports by the status line or by the placeholder line that opens an empty section. In this round each report wrote its status differently, so the search found the placeholder lines, which used the Korean words for "writing" and "in progress". At dca6cf9, over the two folders (analysis and fix reports, device tests), this finds three: the docs consolidation, review and after-fix test reports.
    git grep -lE "^(Status: in progress|\((<writing>|<in progress>))" <commit> -- <report dirs>
  2. See what the previous session changed.
    git diff --stat <start commit>..<partial commit> -- <owned files>
  3. List the raw folder. If a measurement has a suspiciously small n, check the calculation script before measuring again.
  4. Set the report's status to done and add one line on who took over what.

Per-judgment rows are not measured yet

We have not measured how many rows survive an interruption when a read-only task like the string inventory writes one row per judgment.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does a subagent's work survive when it hits a session limit?

On this app, only the files it had already written to disk survived. Of the five agents cut off, all four with a committed report had empty bodies apart from one environment section; four of the five handovers ran on logs, screenshots and edited files, and the fifth had nothing and started over.

What should a subagent prompt state first?

What not to do, where outputs go, and the report format. The shared brief here spent its 33 lines on those three and on environment facts, and each agent's topic was given separately.

Does letting subagents commit solve the interruption problem?

We did not try it. Several agents edited the same working tree at once, so only the main session committed; when an agent was cut off, the main session committed its partial work and said so in the commit message.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Nine auto-compactions in a 13-day Claude Code session, and the memory index line that came back after each one
  • 13 parallel AI agent branches passed review and CI; a review of the merged code still confirmed 12 defects
  • Several Claude Code sessions, one repo: the file owner table, checked against 13 merges

item.title: HWP compatibility test: Save As in Hancom Docs – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

All seven files opened in Hancom Office Viewer with no damage notice. Save As in Hancom Docs needed a sign-in first; both files tried afterwards re-saved, the first (h3) 33 minutes after the production release.

The first screen of Hancom Docs was a sign-in form, and the agent stopped there. On October 18, 2026, on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15), we opened seven HWP files edited with the code of our app HWP Viewer SugarDoc in the two Android apps from Hancom, the company behind the HWP format and the Hangul word processor. All seven opened with no damage notice and their unedited pages matched the originals; only an emoji drew as a blank. Re-saving was tried on two of them, h3 and h7, after the operator signed in, and both passed (171,008 B and 171,520 B).

Sources: the Hancom compatibility QA document, the 1.3.0 release record and the plan and design documents in the app repository (sugar-utils), commits 1b7c328, 36b0dfe, 4628d12 and b7dbf3b, and the work session log from that evening. Checked again on October 31, 2026.

Four pass criteria, and the agent could reach three

Before edit was switched on, the plan held a Hancom compatibility table. Each document gets the body and table-cell edits that apply to it, plus one file with the special characters < & > " ' and an emoji, and one long insertion that pushes text onto a new page. A file passes four checks: (1) it opens with no damage or repair notice, (2) the edited text is visible, (3) unedited pages match the original, (4) Hancom can save it again. Form-field filling had already been cut from the edit scope, for the reasons in We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug, so the form-field column was dropped too.

The table started out as a job for a person. On October 18 the operator handed it to the agent, to run on the S21, and limited it to installing free apps: no payments, no sign-ins. The plan that the agent could finish the table alone broke on check 4. The agent installed Hancom Office Viewer (com.tf.thinkdroid.viewer) and Hancom Docs (com.hancom.docs.suite 2.0.15.544) from Play. Viewer had no save function. Hancom Docs could save, and its first screen asked for a sign-in. At 17:24 the agent took a screenshot of the sign-in screen and backed out.

The test files came from node, running the app's own edit code

The table calls for Korean text and an emoji. adb shell input text, the usual way to type into an app from a script, only takes ASCII, so driving SugarDoc's screen could not produce those files. The agent ran the edit code the app runs inside its WebView (Editor in edit.js: pick a target, apply, then exportChecked to export and reopen) in node, on the same pinned rhwp 0.8.6 engine (measured in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents). Each result then went through the app's Kotlin preview scrub (PreviewScrubber.scrubHwp5) and save gate (HwpExportVerifier.verify); all seven passed. The on-device save path was covered separately that day by a device E2E run that typed ASCII markers.

The generator the agent wrote only picked text runs of two or more characters, and the form document had nothing but empty paragraphs and a form field, so h5 came back with no target (BODY:NONE). It has the same cause as the empty-paragraph case in the save gate note. The agent switched h5 to typing into an empty paragraph, rebuilt the set a minute later, and put the seven files and their originals into Download/HancomCheck/ on the S21.

Eight screenshots per file, and h7 checked by eye

Sending an HWP to Viewer through a VIEW intent made Viewer ask for "All files access". The agent tapped "Later" and found another way in: Viewer's own Open button, which hands off to the system file picker and needs no such permission.

The comparison script opens the original and the edited file the same way, takes eight screenshots at the same scroll steps, and counts pixels whose grayscale difference is above 40. It also searches the screen's view tree for Korean words meaning damaged, repair, error, cannot open and not supported. The first two runs opened nothing, because the picker started in another folder; a step that walks into the folder fixed that. The same swipe does not stop at exactly the same place twice (4 to 16 px apart on files whose pages did not move), so the script slides the edited shot up or down by at most 70 px (staying clear of the status and tool bars) to the best match before counting. Screens with a nonzero count were turned into side-by-side images and reviewed.

FileEditPagesScreens with 0 diffWhere it differed
h1marker text after a body text run3→36/8the edited line and the next one reflowed
h2table cell text3→37/8that cell (1,164 px)
h3body and table cell1→10/8the two edits (4,037 px on each screen)
h4cell and body, document with a form field3→36/8the edits; the form field placeholder unchanged
h5text in an empty paragraph of a form1→10/8the new line (784 px); form objects unchanged
h6special characters and an emoji (U+1F600)3→36/8the edited line; characters shown, emoji blank
h7a sentence of about 480 characters1→20/8everything moved down a page

h3 and h5 are one page long, so all eight screenshots show the same view and catch the same edit each time. No file produced a warning. Viewer also raised nothing about the preview streams, which the app replaces on save (PrvText with spaces, PrvImage with a blank image).

The emoji is still U+1F600 when rhwp reopens the file, yet Viewer drew it as a blank. We had no emoji document authored in Hancom's own software to compare with, so we do not know whether the font or the file is responsible. SugarDoc's edit sheet does not block emoji input.

The release conditions disagreed, and the re-save came after release

At 20:07 the 1.3.0 commit that turned edit on (1b7c328) carried the first version of the QA document: open and display 7 of 7, re-save not checked. It asked the operator to try "Save As" on at least one result file (h3 and h7 suggested) on a signed-in device before release, and to switch edit off (flagEdit=false) if that failed. The agent left edit on because no file had failed; the main session that received its report advised against production until the check was done. The operator approved the production release, and at 20:33 commit 36b0dfe recorded it with "Hancom re-save unverified". The release conditions also differed between documents: the plan listed all four checks and the production ban, while the decision table in the design document only blocked release if check 1 failed.

The agent does not type passwords or create accounts, so it asked the operator to sign in; at 20:57 the operator said the S21 was signed in to Hancom Docs. Hancom Docs then asked for "All files access", and the agent would not switch on a security permission itself. Its first directions pointed to the permission list on the app info screen, and the operator replied that the permission was not there. On this S21 it sat under special access in Settings. The agent opened that settings screen directly with an intent, and the operator switched it on at 21:01.

The first attempt to open the Hancom Docs editor showed Google Play's "app not recognized" screen (the app had been installed from Play). To see whether our file was the cause, the agent opened the unedited original of h3 the same way, through the file manager's "open with". The original opened in the editor, and the Play screen never came back. The record attributes it to a one-off check on Hancom's side; nobody confirmed the cause.

At 21:05 the edited h3 opened in the editor with no damage notice and both edits visible. "Save As" from the menu wrote resave_h3.hwp (171,008 B), which reopened with the same text and layout. h7 opened still pushed from one page to two; resave_h7.hwp (171,520 B) reopened with the two-page layout, table and logo unchanged. Commit 4628d12 recorded both at 21:10.

Do not call a file compatible because it opens. The bar is a re-save in the vendor's app, and if that step sits behind a sign-in, name the person who does that step in the table before the work starts.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Direct editor launch, pixel judging for h7, desktop Hangul: not used

Launching the Hancom Docs editor activity straight from adb would have skipped the file manager, but it was refused with not exported, so the agent went back to the file manager's "open with". In h7 everything moved down, and all eight screens still differed after alignment (168,496 to 221,626 px each), so we dropped the pixel count for that file and judged it from side-by-side images: the table and logo were intact and the text ran onto page 2. Checking in the desktop Hangul word processor was out from the start, because we had no copy to use.

The pixel diff only aligns vertically, and the re-saved files were only reopened

The comparison only aligns vertically. A different zoom level or horizontal offset is not corrected either, so those screens, like the page-shifted h7, need a person comparing them side by side.

Both re-saved files came out smaller than ours (both 235,520 B, from originals of 292,352 B). We never compared their records, so we do not know what went; reopening and reading the text and layout was the whole check. No Korean edit made through SugarDoc's WebView on a phone has been opened in Hancom's apps. Later on the same evening, after the test files were built, the released edit code (1b7c328) stopped offering empty paragraphs without controls as edit targets. The paragraph h5 typed into holds one control (engine query), so that rule does not apply to it. One device (the S21, Android 15) and one Hancom Docs version (2.0.15.544) were used.

Running the same round trip for your own format

  1. Write the table first: one file per kind of edit (body, table cell, special characters, emoji, a long insertion that moves text to the next page, a form document), four checks each. Put a person's name in every cell that needs a sign-in or a special access permission.
  2. Build test files through the same code path as the app, and keep only those that pass the app's save gate. Put each original next to them with an orig_ prefix.
  3. If the vendor app (made by the company behind the format, here Hancom) asks for broad permissions, look for its own Open menu and the system file picker first.
  4. Open original and result the same way, screenshot the same scroll steps, align vertically, count differing pixels. Look by eye at every nonzero screen and at any file whose pages moved.
  5. Search the view tree for warnings such as damage or repair notices.
  6. In the app that can save, use "Save As" to a new name, reopen it, check text and layout, and note the size.
  7. Mark anything you could not run as unchecked, and make sure every document that sets release conditions uses the same checks.
# apps that handle the format; the all-files access settings screen
adb shell cmd package query-activities --brief -a android.intent.action.VIEW \
  -t application/x-hwp -d content://media/external/downloads/1
adb shell am start -a android.settings.MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION \
  -d package:com.hancom.docs.suite
# differing pixels after vertical alignment (margins for a 1080x2400 S21,
# shortened from the session script)
from PIL import Image, ImageChops
def diff(a_png, b_png, top=300, bottom=330):
    A, B = Image.open(a_png).convert("L"), Image.open(b_png).convert("L")
    bot = A.height - bottom
    def count(dy, k=1):
        a = A.crop((0, top, A.width, bot))
        b = B.crop((0, top + dy, B.width, bot + dy))
        if k > 1:
            a = a.resize((a.width // k, a.height // k))
            b = b.resize((b.width // k, b.height // k))
        d = ImageChops.difference(a, b).point(lambda v: 1 if v > 40 else 0)
        return sum(d.getdata())
    ok = [d for d in range(-120, 121, 2)
          if top + d >= 230 and bot + d <= A.height - 260]
    dy = min(ok, key=lambda d: count(d, 4))
    return count(dy), dy

On the S21 the first command listed Hancom Docs and Viewer among the apps that open HWP.

Five files and the desktop word processor are still unchecked

h1, h2, h4, h5 and h6 have not been re-saved in Hancom Docs, and the repository shows no change through its October 29 commits. That set includes the emoji file h6 and h4, the document with a form field. Opening and saving in the desktop Hangul word processor, and the cause of the blank emoji, are also still open.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can Hancom Office Viewer save an HWP file under a new name?

Not the version we used on the S21 on October 18, 2026: it had no save function. We used "Save As" in the Hancom Docs editor after signing in.

Where is "All files access" for Hancom Docs on Android?

On our S21 (Android 15) it was not in the app's permission list but under special access in Settings. Over adb, am start -a android.settings.MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION -d package:com.hancom.docs.suite opens that screen directly.

item.title: HWPX MIME type and Android intent filters – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Method

On Android, HWPX can arrive as application/octet-stream: an 18-row intent matrix and the intent filter that fits it

A viewer that only registers document MIME types misses every .hwpx that arrives as octet-stream. Accept octet-stream through one alias, and decide what the file is from its bytes, not its name.

When we tapped an .hwpx file in Chrome's download list on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15), our viewer received application/octet-stream. Opening the same kind of file from Samsung My Files on the same phone delivered application/vnd.hancom.hwpx. On October 5, 2026 we sent documents to the release build of our HWP viewer, SugarDoc, from different apps and in different ways, wrote down 18 rows of what arrived, and then corrected the manifest against that matrix and the E2E runs that followed. Filling in the matrix turned up one crash on a share sent without a read grant. A day later, accepting octet-stream shares made the app appear twice in the chooser for a */* share.

Sources: the app repository's intent matrix QA document (2026-10-05), on-device E2E reports (Oct 5 to 7), the 1.0.0 release record (Oct 8 and 9), and the manifest and SendEntryActivity code in commit ca1ade4. HWP and HWPX are the document formats of Hancom Office, a Korean word processor.

The same .hwpx came in under two MIME types

Eleven of the 18 rows come from real apps sending a document: Samsung My Files (4 rows), Chrome (4) and Files (3). The other seven are a debug sender app (2) and adb (5). While the reader was on screen we read typ= and flg= from dumpsys activity activities.

Sender (device).hwpx.hwp.pdfNEW_TASK
Samsung My Files (S21)vnd.hancom.hwpxx-hwppdfno (0x3000001)
Chrome download list (S21)octet-streamx-hwpopened by Chromeyes (0x13000003)
Files (emulator, API 35)octet-streamx-hwppdfno (0x23000003)

Each sender gets its MIME type from a different place. Chrome passed on whatever the download server sent. Files (DocumentsUI) relies on the MIME table of the system image, and the emulator image had no entry for hwpx; when we checked the AOSP MIME table on October 4 it listed x-hwp but not hwpx. Only My Files attached a Hancom type. In an engine test on October 3, My Files sent an .hwpx as vnd.hancom.hwpx even though MediaStore had recorded it as application/octet-stream.

Our early research notes assumed that .hwp files arrive as octet-stream too. They don't: in the matrix all three apps sent .hwp as application/x-hwp. Only .hwpx came through as an unknown file, so a viewer that registers only document types opens .hwp yet is missing from the "Open with" list for .hwpx. The user-side fixes are in How to open an HWPX or HWP file on Android.

PDFs from Chrome never reached us. Chrome opened downloaded PDFs in its own viewer, and the "Open" button in the download-complete message only showed the download list. No filter can change that, so the matrix conclusion just notes that a Chrome PDF has to go through My Files.

One alias that takes octet-stream, and a byte check behind it

VIEW is received by a single activity-alias, .reader.OpenUnknownFile. One filter holds the 11 document MIME types and five generic ones. One filter means one entry in the chooser.

<activity-alias android:name=".reader.OpenUnknownFile"
    android:enabled="true" android:exported="true"
    android:targetActivity=".reader.ReaderActivity">
  <intent-filter>
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
    <data android:scheme="content" />
    <!-- 11 document types: pdf, x-pdf, x-hwp, haansofthwp, vnd.hancom.hwp,
         vnd.haansoft-hwp, hwp+zip, x-hwp+zip, haansofthwpx,
         vnd.hancom.hwpx, x-hwpx -->
    <data android:mimeType="application/vnd.hancom.hwpx" />
    <!-- 5 generic types -->
    <data android:mimeType="application/octet-stream" />
    <data android:mimeType="binary/octet-stream" />
    <data android:mimeType="application/x-download" />
    <data android:mimeType="application/download" />
    <data android:mimeType="application/force-download" />
  </intent-filter>
</activity-alias>

x-download is there because on October 4 attachments from korea.kr, a Korean government website, arrived with that type and Chrome did not remap it. Every type is lowercase: the Android documentation says MIME matching in the framework is case-sensitive.

Taking octet-stream puts the app in the chooser for every unnamed file, so the reader reads the first 64 KB and decides the format from bytes, copying the whole file first when the proof sits further in. A PDF needs %PDF- in its first 1 KB. HWP 5 needs a CFB container whose FileHeader says "HWP Document File". HWPX needs a ZIP whose first entry is a stored mimetype reading application/hwp+zip. HWP 3 has its own signature. The MIME type and file name can only soften a verdict, never create one. On a local set of 635 files (255 documents, the rest files that must be rejected) the check made no wrong calls.

The last two matrix rows test this on a device. We built a 4 KiB file with an m4a header (ftyp M4A) and sent it named .hwp with type application/x-hwp. On the S21 the chooser started 197 to 215 ms after the VIEW; with only one other app able to take the file, the system went straight to the phone's other office viewer, and no copy stayed in our app. The emulator has no other app that takes HWP, so there we sent the same file as application/pdf; the hand-off to Google Drive's PDF viewer took 435 ms.

A share without a read grant crashed SendEntryActivity

Shares (SEND) land in SendEntryActivity, which has no UI: it forwards to the reader in onCreate and finishes. In one adb row of the October 5 matrix we shared a PDF with only EXTRA_STREAM and no --grant-read-uri-permission. The activity died with a SecurityException and took the process with it.

  1. The sender passed a URI but no read permission for it.
  2. The code the agent wrote added FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION to the intent it forwarded to the reader, trying to pass on a grant the app never held.
  3. The system refused that startActivity with a SecurityException, the exception escaped onCreate, and the process went down.

The fix, SendForward, catches only that exception and forwards again without the grant flag and without ClipData. The reader then tries the URI and, if it can't read it, shows the "can't access" screen (E1).

fun start(forward: Intent, start: (Intent) -> Unit) {
    try {
        start(forward)
    } catch (e: SecurityException) {
        start(withoutGrant(forward))  // drop the grant flag and ClipData
    }
}

A JVM test (SendForwardTest) pins this down, and the device smoke script's send_twice step sends an ungranted SEND on every run. In the 1.0.0 (3) regression on October 8, the eight smoke checks that include this step passed 8 of 8 on both the S21 (Android 15) and the S20 (Android 13). In the matrix only the adb row with the grant removed produced the crash; none of the real-app rows did. We don't know which apps, if any, share this way.

Adding a SEND alias listed the app twice

In the E2E run of October 5 and 6, the entry-intents-10 scenario (a simulated mail share) drew the first page in 21 of 25 cases on the S21 and 20 of 25 on the S20 in its final round. Every failure was an .hwpx shared as octet-stream, because the first design accepted SEND only for the 11 document types. The E2E report suggested deciding after measuring real mail apps; on October 6 the operator chose to accept octet-stream shares first, and the code comment records the reason as "mail apps share .hwpx that way".

The agent added a new alias, SendUnknownFile, for octet-stream shares. After that, a share typed */* matched both the existing SendEntryActivity filter and the new alias, because Android matches a */* intent against any typed filter. The S20 chooser showed two identical "SugarDoc" entries; on the S21 an extra one-item resolver step appeared.

On October 7 we changed it so that only one component is enabled for any given intent. SendEntryActivity lost its filter and became exported=false, and SEND now goes through one of two aliases: SendUnknownFile (11 document types plus octet-stream) while the setting is on, SendDocument (11 types) while it is off. After SEND was fixed, the recheck found that VIEW */* also matched both ReaderActivity and OpenUnknownFile, a layout that had been there since the October 5 matrix. Tests assumed the ReaderActivity filter, so it was set aside at first and given the same treatment later that day. When the setting changes, the alias taking over is enabled before the other is disabled, so there can briefly be two entries but never zero.

We checked with cmd package query-activities. On the S21 release build with the setting on, VIEW for */*, pdf, hwpx and octet-stream all resolved to OpenUnknownFile alone; with it off, to ViewDocument alone, and octet-stream to nothing. A recheck the same day showed one "SugarDoc" in both the "Open with" and the share choosers.

Keep exactly one enabled component per action for each MIME type.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Why not */*, pathPattern, or off by default

We never declared a */* filter; it would put a document viewer in the list for every photo and recording. Octet-stream carries the same risk on a smaller scale, limited to unnamed files, and the byte check hands non-documents straight on. application/zip and application/unknown stay out until a real app is seen sending them.

Matching .hwpx with pathPattern doesn't work for content URIs. My Files handed us a URI shaped like content://media/external/file/N, with no file name in the path. The Android documentation says the path attributes of <data> mean something only when the filter names a host. You can widen the host to * so the path condition applies to any sender, but a URI like that has no extension in its path to match. On October 4 we read a competing app's manifest: it accepted octet-stream only under a pathPattern, and its reviews included complaints that .hwpx didn't appear in the "Open with" list. That link between the manifest and the reviews is our inference.

Shipping the generic alias switched off was the other option. In the matrix, turning the setting off and sending an octet-stream VIEW removed the app from the chooser, so off by default means .hwpx from Chrome and Files never lists us. On October 5 the operator approved on by default. The decision table weighed being listed in "Open with" against backlash at an app that grabs files. The setting "Show for all file types" lets users turn it off, and the product spec says a high rejection rate on the generic alias sends us back to off by default or to fewer MIME types.

KakaoTalk opened the files, but nobody wrote down the MIME type

The agent could not test KakaoTalk, Korea's main messaging app: a second account has to send the file. The matrix put KakaoTalk, Naver Mail (a Korean webmail service) and Gmail in a separate table of checks for the owner. The October 9 release record has the operator's result: on a Galaxy S23, four test folders sent from another KakaoTalk account (an HWPX official letter, an HWP5 official letter, a PDF and an old HWP3 file) all opened in the viewer. The record has no MIME type and no NEW_TASK flag. Today's filter takes both the document types and octet-stream, so the fact that the files opened doesn't tell us which one KakaoTalk used.

The device coverage is narrow too. The matrix ran on the S21 (Android 15) and an API 35 emulator, and the regression added the S20 (Android 13). We didn't look at other manufacturers' file apps, and Files by Google wasn't installed on any test device.

Building the same intent matrix for your app with adb

  1. Open an .hwpx, an .hwp and a .pdf from each sender. While your reader is on screen, record the MIME type, flags and authority. Leave file names out.
    adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -A3 <package>
  2. Count how many times your package matches each type. For VIEW and SEND alike, */*, each document type and octet-stream should give exactly one.
    adb shell cmd package query-activities --brief \
  -a android.intent.action.VIEW -t '*/*' -d content://x/y
  3. Share without a read grant. The app must not crash; it should end on its "can't access" screen.
    adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.SEND \
  -t application/pdf --eu android.intent.extra.STREAM <content URI>
  4. VIEW a non-document, such as an m4a, named .hwp with a document MIME type. Check that it goes to the chooser and that no copy stays in app storage.
  5. Turn the generic-type setting off and send an octet-stream VIEW. Your app should be missing from the chooser and come back when the setting is on again.
  6. Messenger and mail apps need a second account to send from.

The engine side is in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents, and the same app's PDF path problem is in androidx.pdf beta01 runs your Application.onCreate a second time, in an isolated process, and the PDF silently never opens.

Next: mail app MIME types, and the setting under an open reader

We haven't opened a Naver Mail or Gmail attachment yet. Mail apps were the stated reason for accepting octet-stream shares, so recording their MIME types with dumpsys comes first. We also haven't tried switching the setting while a reader opened through the alias that gets disabled is still on screen; the system might close that reader, or returning to it from Recents might fail. The rule to roll back on a high rejection rate is written down, but there is no record yet of anyone reading that number.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

What is the MIME type of an .hwpx file on Android?

It depends on the sending app. On October 5, 2026, Samsung My Files sent application/vnd.hancom.hwpx, while Chrome's download list and Files on the emulator sent application/octet-stream. Our filter lists application/haansofthwpx, application/vnd.hancom.hwpx, application/x-hwpx, application/hwp+zip and octet-stream together.

Can I match .hwpx with pathPattern in an intent filter?

Not for content URIs. The URI Samsung My Files handed us, content://media/external/file/N, carries no file name to match. Match on MIME type and check the bytes.

item.title: Parallel AI agent branches: 12 integration defects – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

13 parallel AI agent branches passed review and CI; a review of the merged code still confirmed 12 defects

Every branch had its own agent review and green CI. A separate review of the merged code still confirmed 12 defects the existing tests had not caught; by our count, 10 sat between two packages.

Six review agents that read only the merged code reported 2 blockers and 10 majors, and the agents assigned to refute them could not knock down a single one. Before that, each of the 13 feature branches had been reviewed by three adversarial agents and had green CI. This happened in the early hours of October 10, 2026 (Korea time), while merging the first parallel wave (Wave 1) of AXFamily, our family calendar app. None of the 12 were caught by the existing tests or showed up as a git conflict. By our classification, 10 of the 12 were broken agreements between code written by two different packages.

Sources: git history (merges 58920b9 to ff0c975, a0351cf, 941d79e, c153fae, 74d3685, 5d51b5b, cee9d0f), the descriptions of the integration PR and the billing package PR, the fix report, and the integration workflow script with its run log (each agent's findings and refutation verdict). Times are KST. Rechecked on 2026-10-31.

From the 01:51 merges to the 05:34 PR merge

Wave 1 ran one workflow that put every package through the same steps: one agent implemented it, three agents reviewed the branch through security, cost and correctness lenses, and a fix agent addressed their findings and got the PR to green CI. The two-minute merge of all 13 branches starting at 01:51, and the minimal fixes for 6 package pairs in a0351cf at 02:09, are covered in Claude Code sessions in one repo: file owner table.

Three wiring commits followed to apply the lead session's cross-package decisions, in the order contract, server, app (941d79e at 02:53, c153fae at 03:42, 74d3685 at 04:23). The code the review read included those wiring commits.

The six reviewers started together at 04:29 and finished within 6 to 9 minutes, making 30 to 95 tool calls each. At 04:38 each of the 12 blocker and major findings went to its own refuting agent, and within a minute all 12 came back as real. The fix agent pushed 5d51b5b at 05:28 (115 files, 2,088 lines added). Once all 11 CI jobs passed, the integration PR was merged into develop at 05:34.

The first assumption: green tests meant the integration was done

The plan described Wave 1 as "parallel feature work (separate files only)", and its conflict rules were written per shared file. The integration step was told to resolve conflicts keeping both sides' intent, run every test suite, and fix integration breakage minimally.

The integration agent finished by that standard. Its PR description said it had fixed only what the integration broke, and listed the numbers: 977 Flutter tests, 274 function unit tests and 291 emulator tests, 441 Rules tests (5 skipped) and 132 media Worker tests, all passing. None of the 12 defects found later changed any of those numbers. The lead session had put a review step at the end of the workflow, and that step is where the defects appeared.

32 findings from six lenses; 12 survived refutation

The six lenses were Rules and contract, function security, cost, app security and privacy, app UX, and flow tracing, which followed the core user flow in code from sign-in to account deletion. They reported 32 findings: 20 minor and 12 blocker or major. The cost lens reported only 3 minor findings. One finding from Rules and contract and one from function security were the same defect, found from both sides, so there were 11 distinct defects.

The refutation prompt told each agent to read the code and refute the finding, defaulting to "not real" unless the defect could be shown. Each refuter made 3 to 6 tool calls and returned a verdict in 16 to 25 seconds. The verdicts cited files and line numbers; the one on the missing index pointed out that comments and assets, queried the same way, already had their composite indexes.

By our count, 10 of the 12 sat between two packages

Rewriting each confirmed defect as "which two pieces of code believed different things" gives the table below. The classification is ours, made while writing this note; it is not in the original records. App feature details are kept short.

Lens (severity)The two sidesThe mismatch
Rules and contract, function security (major, same defect twice)Rules vs. a function added during wiringRules let any adult in the household edit a list field that the function trusted as proof of consent eligibility
Rules and contract (major)Records screen query vs. index fileNo composite index for a sorted query
Function security (major)Revocation check vs. ownership transferA revocation was re-evaluated against the revoker's current role, so a role change undid it
App security and privacy (major)Records device cleanup vs. sign-out cleanup registryCleanup never registered; it ran only asynchronously and never retried
App security and privacy (major)Inside the share inbox storeCopied files left behind when the queue passed 100 items or got corrupted
App UX (blocker)Billing entry widget vs. family screenZero production callers of the widget
App UX (major)Household deletion function vs. settings screenThe app never sent the server's cancel flag and parsed the cancelled reply as an error
App UX (major)UI spec vs. bottom action buttonButton shown on tabs the spec excluded, with the wrong label
App UX (major)Banner slot vs. screen state reportsOne failure blocked banners for the whole session (spec says per screen); cached offline screens reported ready
Flow tracing (blocker)App capture vs. AI extraction functionFor PDF sources the app sent image/webp; the server accepted only application/pdf
Flow tracing (major)Household picker vs. today/calendar screens and billingThe picker wrote a new key, the screens read an old key nothing wrote, billing used the first household

Only two stayed inside one package: the share inbox files and the bottom button. In the other 10 (9 distinct defects), each side was correct on its own. In the PDF case, the app sent a first-page thumbnail exactly as its own code comment said, and the server counted pages from PDF bytes exactly as the contract said at the time.

Each branch review read only its own diff

The branch review prompt had each reviewer read git diff origin/develop...origin/<branch>. The index file already existed on develop, and the Rules package was changing it on its own branch, but it never appeared in the diff read by the agent reviewing the records screen's sorted query. The same held for app capture: the server check that accepts only application/pdf for PDF sources was already on develop, but not in that reviewer's diff.

The billing package's review had already found one of these defects. In that branch review, the correctness lens had been told to grep for production callers of every new API, the same rule the operator now keeps in the global instructions for all projects. That review did find that nothing called the billing entry widget, but rated it minor; the billing re-review just before integration raised it to major. The call belonged in the family screen file, which the file owner rules kept the billing fix agent from touching, so the agent put the item in the PR description's "to align with other packages" section, marked as required at integration. The integration workflow's wiring task list was already written into the script when it launched at 01:28, before the billing re-review finished. The item came back as a blocker in the integration review that started at 04:29.

Tests ran per package against that package's own fakes and the Firestore emulator. As the comment at the top of the index test file already said, the Firestore emulator does not enforce composite indexes. The contract's query table listed sources among the list queries, but the required composite index list in the same section left sources out. CI passed, and only the production Firestore would have answered with FAILED_PRECONDITION. (The review caught it before any production deploy, so it never actually happened.)

Agent-written code and tests also hid mismatches. A comment in the today/calendar code said the active-household key was "written by A1's household switcher" (A1 being the family screen package), but git grep found no code anywhere that wrote that key. The bottom button test was named "the FAB is on every tab"; it locked in the placement and label the spec had ruled out.

After merging parallel branches, run a review that reads only the merged code, however many branch reviews came before.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The check we kept: a sorted-query-to-index table

According to the fix report, 5d51b5b added for each defect a test written to fail on the code before the fix; the Rules, index and consent fixes were actually reverted to watch the tests fail. (The revert technique is in Finding fake tests by deleting their guards.) Two of the fixes were turned into checks for the next mismatch of the same kind.

For indexes, the Rules test suite gained a table of app queries that use orderBy. Each row names the app file, the query and the index it needs, and the test looks for that index in the index file. A final test counts how often orderBy: ' appears in each listed file and compares that with the number of table rows, then compares the list of app files containing the string with the table's files. Anyone adding a sorted query has to add a row first.

const count = (rel) => (readFileSync(resolve(appRoot, rel), 'utf8').match(/orderBy:\s*'/g) ?? []).length;
// …
expect(actual).toEqual(expected);
// fail if a file outside the table uses orderBy: '<field>'
const all = execSync(`grep -rlE "^\\s*orderBy: '" lib || true`, { cwd: appRoot, encoding: 'utf8' })
  .split('\n').filter(Boolean).map((f) => f.trim());
expect(all.sort()).toEqual(files.sort());

By October 13, three more app files with sorted queries had been added to the table. The history does not show whether the table check failed first and forced those rows. For household selection, the fix made the app session's current household the single source of truth; with two or more households and no valid selection, the picker returns null instead of falling back to the first one. Three tests pin that rule.

Other routes: a staging project, shared test vectors

A real Firestore project would have exposed the missing index at once. The plan had postponed a staging project until after launch, citing low benefit for the risk and one more place that could incur charges. The device end-to-end runs that same morning used an emulator backend to keep costs at zero, so they would not have shown it either.

One method had already worked. The billing package's tests were written to read a shared vector file (expected results for whether a subscription counts as active) that the billing server package would add, and skipped themselves with "runs automatically once merged" while the file was missing from develop. Right after the merge, that test ran and caught the app and server disagreeing on the entitlement check, which a0351cf fixed. Contracts without a vector file, like consent eligibility or household selection, could not be caught by that test.

What a read-only review missed: three device E2E rounds

Three rounds of device E2E, run after the E2E harness commit at 07:37 the same day, found more runtime defects. One of them, d3fde30, fixed Firestore triggers that crashed without a default Admin app, and the 5d51b5b fix report itself says the Android side got Kotlin unit tests only. Why device checks run separately even after a review converges on zero is covered in Agent code review: fix what survives refutation.

Each finding got one refuter for 16 to 25 seconds, so 12 out of 12 surviving is not evidence that refutation can be dropped. The app UX lens was told to compare screens against the written UI spec, and the button and banner findings cited spec clauses. In a project without a written spec, that lens has nothing to compare against.

How to run integration review as its own step

  1. Collect every branch PR's "to align with other packages" list into the integration task list. Finalize the wiring list only after every branch review is done.
  2. Once everything is merged and all suites are green, hand the integration diff to one read-only agent per area, asking for concrete defects with evidence only and for each one to be refuted by the reviewer before it is reported. AXFamily's six lenses were Rules and contract, function security, cost, app security and privacy, app UX (screens vs. the UI spec), and flow tracing (sign-in to account deletion).
    git diff --stat origin/develop...origin/<integration-branch>
  3. Count production callers for every new widget, function and parameter, excluding the file that defines it. Zero is a finding by itself.
    git grep -n "BillingPlanRow(" -- apps/app/lib ':!apps/app/lib/features/billing/plan_row.dart'
  4. Send each blocker and major to a different agent to refute, and drop anything it cannot be shown (the procedure is in Agent code review: fix what survives refutation).
  5. For each confirmed defect, add a test that fails on the old code, and revert the fix once to watch it fail.
  6. Turn each defect type into a check: a table check when both sides can be counted, like queries and indexes; a shared vector file read by both sides' tests when it is a decision rule.

Next to check: server queries and gaps in the table

The sorted-query table counts only the orderBy: ' string in app code. Server function queries were still added to the required index list by hand on October 13, and the shape of each where clause depends on whoever writes the row. Whether server queries can be counted the same way is the next thing to try.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

If every branch had an AI review, do I still need an integration review?

You still need one. In AXFamily every branch was reviewed by three agents, and the merged code still had 12 blocker or major defects, 10 of them spanning two packages by our count. A branch review reads only that branch's diff, so it misses the other side of a contract whenever that side is not in the diff.

Will Firestore emulator tests catch a missing composite index?

The emulator does not enforce composite indexes, so tests pass with the index missing. Add a static check that matches the app's sorted queries against the index file, or run the queries against a real project.

How long did the integration review take?

Review took 6 to 9 minutes and refutation under a minute; the fix took about 49 minutes to its commit and about 55 minutes to the PR merge after CI. Counting the merges and wiring before it, the whole run from the 01:51 merges to the 05:34 PR merge took 3 hours 43 minutes.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: AXFamily: shared family calendar and AI assistant – SugarMount
item.description:
AXFamily

AXFamily is an Android shared family calendar that gathers your family's events and to-dos in one place and shows who is taking care of each one.

Coming soon

AXFamily privacy policy

Use it to

  • Stop sorting out school notices and class schedules over chat every time
  • Share childcare with grandparents and decide who takes care of what
  • Plan a trip with kids around nap and meal times

What it does

  • Decide who does what

    Tap "I'll do it" on a to-do so your family sees who's on it, or "Can't do it" when you can't. Check off things to bring one by one, and turn on notifications for reminders before events.

  • A heads-up every Sunday evening

    With notifications on, every Sunday evening you see to-dos nobody took, overlapping events, deadlines and birthdays within 7 days. The list is free and doesn't count toward AI uses.

  • Dates and things to bring from a notice photo

    Upload a photo of a school notice and AI finds its dates and things to bring. It is added only after you check it and tap Save.

  • Ask the AI assistant

    Open "Ask the family" and ask "What am I in charge of this week?" It answers from your family's events and to-dos, shows which record it used, and says so if there's none. Ask it to add an event and it drafts one; it's saved only when you tap Save.

  • Trip and weekend helper

    Pick where, when and who's going for a day-by-day plan, with packing, a budget and who does what. It fits around your kids' nap, meal and bed times, and marks opening hours, prices and travel times "Check details". The plan is added only after every adult on the trip says yes.

  • Family memories

    Within a week after a trip or event, it suggests an album of its events and photos. Ask "When was our beach trip last year?" to find it. Only records of adults who agreed to AI are used.

  • Your items stay yours

    New events and records start private. Share them with the whole family or chosen people, or pick "Time only" to show when you're busy, not what it is. No one else, even the family admin, sees your private items, not even through the AI.

At a glance

StatusComing soon
FamilyAdults join from an invite message. Kids are added as profiles, no sign-in or phone needed.
AccountGoogle account or email, age 19 or older
PlansEvents, to-dos, reminders, the Sunday heads-up and sharing settings are free (5 AI uses a month, 1,000 photos, one banner ad). Family Plus subscription: no ads, 150 AI uses a month, 10,000 photos
AIGoogle's Gemini model. Each adult turns it on with their own consent.
InternetNeeded (records are shared with your family).
LanguagesKorean and English
Android12L or later
Package namecom.sugarmount.axfamily
Developersimpest (SugarMount)

Data and permissions

  • Family records are never shared with advertisers. Personalized ads are shown only if you agree.
  • Photos are uploaded as small copies without location data. Originals stay on your phone.
  • For children under 14, names and notes aren't sent to the AI. Events and trips a child joins use an age group (like "elementary") instead of a name.
  • Health records are not sent to the AI unless you turn them on, and then only your own.
  • Delete your account and records in the app's Settings or from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions in Google Play.

See AXFamily privacy policy for details.

What it can't do

  • AXFamily is in internal testing and not yet public on Google Play.
  • AI can be wrong. AI text is labeled "AI-generated"; always check opening hours, prices and travel times yourself.
  • AI uses are shared by the family and refill on the 1st of each month. Daily limits apply (20 per person, 30 per family).
  • AXFamily isn't made by a school. Upload the notices you receive yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Do kids need an account?

No. Kids are added as profiles without signing in, and they don't need a phone. Accounts are for adults aged 19 or older.

Can I use it without AI?

Yes. Events, to-dos and reminders all work without AI. AI turns on only for adults who each agree to it.

Can my partner see my private events?

No. Items you keep private can't be seen by anyone else, even the family admin, and don't show up when someone else asks the AI.

How do I delete my account?

Delete it in the app's Settings or request it from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions separately in Google Play.

Related apps

  • SugarSpeller
  • SugarClip
  • HWP Viewer SugarDoc
